```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(OncoCohortSelect)
```

OncoCohortSelect compares single-arm cohorts with several efficacy and safety
endpoints, for example two combination regimens studied in parallel cohorts of
a phase 2 trial, by two approaches:

* a posterior benefit-risk score (Chakraborty et al., 2026), computed for each
  cohort against target values or for one cohort relative to another, and
* generalized pairwise comparisons of prioritized endpoints (Buyse, 2010),
  which give the net treatment benefit, the win ratio and the win odds.

The same functions are used for the data of a completed trial and for
simulated trials. This vignette analyzes one simulated trial; the vignette
"Comparing selection rules by simulation" evaluates the two approaches.

## Data

Each cohort is described by an `OncoArm` object of the CorOncoEndpoints
package, which generates progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS)
and objective response with the association between them. `SimCohorts()` adds
a binary adverse event, independent of the other endpoints, and cuts the data
at the calendar time of the analysis. Here 50 patients per cohort are enrolled
over 12 months and analyzed at month 24.

```{r}
arms <- list(
  Cohort1 = CorOncoEndpoints::OncoArm(pfs.median = 8, orr = 0.45, resp.cor = 0.4,
                                      death.prop = 0.15, os.median = 18),
  Cohort2 = CorOncoEndpoints::OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.4,
                                      death.prop = 0.15, os.median = 15))
d <- SimCohorts(nsim = 1, n = c(50, 50), arms = arms, ae.rate = c(0.35, 0.20),
                cutoff = 24, a.time = c(0, 12), seed = 1)
head(d)
```

The endpoints are defined by the columns that hold them and by their favorable
direction. Any number of endpoints can be defined.

```{r}
eps <- list(
  Endpoint("OS", "tte", time = "os_tte", event = "os_event"),
  Endpoint("PFS", "tte", time = "pfs_tte", event = "pfs_event"),
  Endpoint("ORR", "binary", var = "response"),
  Endpoint("AE", "binary", var = "ae", higher.better = FALSE))
```

## Posterior benefit-risk score

Each row of the criteria defines a component: the posterior probability that
an endpoint is favorable. Response and adverse event rates have beta priors
(by default `Beta(0.5, 0.5)`); for PFS and OS the event times are taken as
exponential with a gamma prior of the hazard (by default shape 0.5 and rate
0), and the parameter is the survival probability at a given time. The
composite score is the weighted geometric mean of the components, and a cohort
is admissible when every component with a cutoff reaches it.

```{r}
crit <- data.frame(endpoint = c("ORR", "PFS", "OS", "AE"),
                   target = c(0.30, 0.50, 0.60, 0.30),
                   time = c(NA, 6, 12, NA),
                   cutoff = c(0.50, 0.50, NA, 0.50))
br <- BenefitRisk(d, eps, crit)
br
sel <- if (any(br$selected)) br$group[br$selected] else "none (no cohort is admissible)"
```

`ORR` is `P(ORR >= 0.3)`, `PFS_S6` is `P(S(6) >= 0.5)` for PFS, `OS_S12` is
`P(S(12) >= 0.6)` for OS and `AE` is `P(AE rate <= 0.3)`. The admissible
cohort with the highest score is selected; here it is `r sel`.
Because each component is the probability of exceeding a fixed target, the
components of a cohort that clearly exceeds all targets are close to 1, and the
score then separates cohorts little.

With a reference cohort, each component is the probability of a difference
from the reference: a margin for a rate or a survival probability, or a bound
for the hazard ratio.

```{r}
crit_ref <- data.frame(endpoint = c("ORR", "PFS", "OS", "AE"),
                       measure = c("rate", "hr", "hr", "rate"),
                       target = c(0.10, 0.80, 0.90, 0.10))
BenefitRisk(d, eps, crit_ref, reference = "Cohort2")
```

Here `ORR` is `P(ORR1 - ORR2 >= 0.1)`, `PFS_HR` and `OS_HR` are the
probabilities that the hazard ratios of Cohort1 versus Cohort2 are at most 0.8
and 0.9, and `AE` is `P(AE1 - AE2 <= 0.1)`.

## Win statistics

Every patient of Cohort1 is compared with every patient of Cohort2, first on
OS, then on PFS (both by the rule of Gehan), then on response and finally on
the adverse event.

```{r}
w <- WinStat(d, eps, treatment = "Cohort1", control = "Cohort2")
w$ci
w$by.endpoint
```

Of the `r w$n[["pairs"]]` pairs, `r round(100 * w$estimate[["p_win"]], 1)`%
are won and `r round(100 * w$estimate[["p_loss"]], 1)`% lost by the patient of
Cohort1, which gives a win ratio of `r round(w$estimate[["wr"]], 2)`.
`by.endpoint` shows how many pairs each endpoint decides: an endpoint lower in
the priority order can only decide the pairs left undecided by the endpoints
above it. The priority order and thresholds for the time-to-event endpoints
are set by `priority` and `threshold`:

```{r}
WinStat(d, eps, treatment = "Cohort1", control = "Cohort2",
        priority = c("ORR", "PFS", "AE", "OS"), threshold = c(0, 2, 0, 0))$by.endpoint
```

## References

Buyse, M. (2010). Generalized pairwise comparisons of prioritized outcomes in
the two-sample problem. *Statistics in Medicine*, 29, 3245-3257.
https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.3923

Chakraborty, S., Dubey, A. K., Kumar, A. and Chan, I. (2026). A two-stage dose
optimization framework for oncology drug development with multiple efficacy
and safety endpoints via an integrated benefit-risk assessment. *Statistics in
Biopharmaceutical Research*, published online.
https://doi.org/10.1080/19466315.2026.2668381
